speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It is certainly the more popular thing to do if we just keep all bus services intact, even if their ridership levels have fallen significantly, while adding new MRT lines and introducing new bus services and routes to serve residents from new estates.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: And the cost increase will then result in higher fares for commuters and larger subsidies paid by taxpayers.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This is the trade-off that we face, between providing convenience for commuters and keeping the overall costs affordable for commuters and taxpayers.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: So, when we argue against changing existing bus services which run parallel to new MRT lines and have experienced significant reductions in ridership levels, we must also be honest in acknowledging that such proposals will come with a price tag.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It is not correct to only focus on the convenience for some commuters without recognising that such an approach will end up with higher fares for all our commuters and higher subsidies that all taxpayers have to bear.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: And if so, what were the results and what were the reasons why one mode was preferred over another?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In response to the Minister's question, I would also offer the point whether the Ministry of Transport (MOT) has considered the cost to the economy, to our environment, if people avoid taking public transport and they choose to continue driving cars or taking other forms of private transport?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: That entails a cost as well and has MOT calculated the cost of that if, let us say, public transport is not as convenient or is perceived to be not as convenient as it was before?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I will still put it to him one more time because I do want to know what his position is – which is that, if we just do what is popular, we keep all the existing bus services intact, even when the ridership levels have fallen significantly, when they run parallel to new MRT lines and we keep introducing new bus services to serve new routes, to serve new residents from new estates, would that not then lead to overall cost for the public transport system increasing?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And if so, then, that means that it would translate into higher fares for commuters and higher subsidies that all taxpayers have to pay.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, I would like to get a reply from Mr Giam on what his position is on my question.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I think I have explained this to Mr Giam previously in this House.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: These are not decisions that we take automatically; just because there is a new MRT line that comes up, automatically or immediately you would remove some of these existing bus services.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Because we understand that there is an impact on commuters.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, therefore, we would have to look at whether there are other bus services that are serving these routes that run parallel to the MRT.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Because I think that is one of the most objective ways of assessing whether commuters still prefer to take this bus service or are commuters then switching to other bus services or are commuters switching to taking MRT.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, for cases where the bus service has experienced a significant drop in ridership level because commuters are now shifting to other modes of public transport – not in the way that Mr Giam has described, in that they avoid taking public transport, I do not think that is the case because the overall public transport ridership level has not dropped.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But what we see is people now switching to taking other bus services or they switch to taking MRT.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And in some cases, when you switch to taking the MRT, it is actually faster for the commuter because the travelling time is more direct.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And this includes walking, taking the bus and taking MRT.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It is still faster than taking a direct, long trunk bus route.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: In contrast, Bus 167 was removed and now it has been brought back, possibly because of public pressure.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: What was the second point that the Minister was asking me about?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Does that answer the question that the Minister was asking me?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: There will be new routes that will be required.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I just want to say that I did not call Mr Giam a populist.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And this is to serve commuters who travel between Bedok Reservoir Road and Bedok interchange, where there are other bus options.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: He said that when there is a choice between taking MRT and a bus on a parallel route, it is faster to take the MRT in many cases.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: The lived reality for a lot of residents, especially the elderly, is that speed is not the highest priority.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Very often, it is if they can walk less and there is a sheltered way all the way that they can take without having to get wet, they would prefer to take the bus rather than MRT.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: I am not saying that we do not get rid of the buses which have low ridership.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: But I think the fact is that we cannot just look in terms of efficiency, in terms of the speed of the trip, because different commuters have different priorities.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: First, I did not say that we only look at efficiency and just because the MRT is a more direct and faster route, therefore, we remove all buses.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, on that front, I do not think Mr Giam and I differ that much in terms of the approach that we want to take.
